A foregone conclusion is an outcome or result that is so certain and predictable that it feels like it has already been decided, even before it actually happens. There is no real suspense, no genuine doubt — everyone can see where things are heading, and the final result is basically a formality.

Think of it this way: if you watch a chess match where one player has already lost their queen, both rooks, and most of their pieces, the other player's victory is a foregone conclusion. The game isn't technically over yet, but the outcome is as good as sealed.

To truly understand this idiom, it helps to look at the two key words:

  • "Foregone" — This comes from the old verb forego, meaning "to go before" or "to precede." So "foregone" means "that which has already passed or been decided beforehand." (Be careful: this is different from "forgo," which means "to give something up." They look similar but mean completely different things.)
  • "Conclusion" — This simply means a result, decision, or ending.

Put them together: a foregone conclusion is literally "a result that has already been gone through beforehand" — in other words, a result that was decided before anyone even finished deliberating.

This phrase was invented by William Shakespeare in his famous tragedy Othello, written around 1603. In the play, the villain Iago manipulates Othello into believing his wife has been unfaithful, and Othello uses the phrase to refer to something that seems already confirmed in his mind.

Interestingly, Shakespeare's original usage had a slightly more specific meaning — referring to something that had literally been experienced or gone through in advance. Over the centuries, the phrase evolved into its modern, broader meaning: any outcome that seems inevitable or already decided.

The fact that this phrase has survived for over 400 years and is still used in everyday English today tells you how powerful and useful it is.

This idiom is not just about certainty — it also carries a particular emotional tone depending on the context:

  • Resignation — Sometimes people use it with a sense of "well, we already knew this would happen," as if the process in between was pointless.
  • Frustration or Sarcasm — If someone goes through a big show of pretending to deliberate when the decision was clearly already made, calling it "a foregone conclusion" can be a subtle way of pointing out that the whole process was fake or hollow.
  • Simple Confidence — Other times, it's used in a neutral or even positive way, simply to acknowledge that something is extremely likely.

The idiom itself is neither positive nor negative — the tone depends entirely on the situation.

Here are several examples across different areas of life, so you can see how naturally it fits into conversation:

Sports:

"Once their star striker got injured in the first half, the defeat was a foregone conclusion."

Politics:

"With such overwhelming support in the polls, her re-election was a foregone conclusion long before voting day."

Work/Business:

"After the audit revealed those financial irregularities, the CEO's resignation was a foregone conclusion."

Everyday life:

"He had been practicing piano for ten years, so winning the competition felt like a foregone conclusion to everyone who knew him."

Sarcastic use:

"They held a three-hour meeting to decide whether to keep their most profitable product. A foregone conclusion dressed up as a debate."

In every case, notice that the result was expected by everyone well in advance, and the eventual outcome simply confirmed what people already knew.
How Certain Does Something Have to Be?

This is an important nuance. A foregone conclusion does not just mean "something that is likely." It means something that is virtually certain — so predictable that calling it a surprise would be absurd. The doubt is basically zero, or close to it.

For example:

  • If your team has a 60% chance of winning a game → that is not a foregone conclusion.
  • If your team is playing against opponents who have already lost five players to injury and are down 5–0 in the last minute → that is a foregone conclusion.

The phrase implies that the outcome is already written, even if the last few formalities haven't played out yet.

Avoid confusing "a foregone conclusion" with these similar-sounding but different ideas:

  • "A lucky guess" — A foregone conclusion isn't a guess at all. It's a certainty backed by clear evidence or overwhelming circumstances.
  • "A self-fulfilling prophecy" — That's when your belief in an outcome causes it to happen. A foregone conclusion is simply one that was always going to happen, regardless of your belief.
  • "A snap judgment" — That's a quick decision made without much thought. A foregone conclusion is about a predictable outcome, not about how fast a decision is made.

These words and phrases carry a similar meaning and can sometimes be used in place of "a foregone conclusion":

  • A certainty — the outcome is sure
  • A done deal — it's already decided (slightly more informal)
  • Inevitable (adjective) — it cannot be avoided
  • A sure thing — informal; very likely to happen
  • Written in the stars — fate has already decided it
  • A no-brainer — so obvious there's nothing to think about (though this leans more toward easy decisions than certain outcomes)

ConceptDetail

"A foregone conclusion" means: the result was never really in doubt. It was predictable, obvious, and effectively decided before the process even finished. You use it when an outcome is so clear that going through the motions feels almost unnecessary. It's a phrase born from Shakespeare, refined over 400 years, and still alive and well in modern English — because the idea of an inevitable outcome is something every human being understands.
